name: Dearborn Street Drawbridge
aka: the first drawbridge across the Chicago River

documented_range.note: THE OPENING IS DISPUTED BY TEN WEEKS AND THE DISPUTE IS BETWEEN THE BUILDER AND HIS COMPILER. Nelson R. Norton, the ship-carpenter who built it, in a letter Andreas prints: 'I came to Chicago November 16, 1833. Soon after I arrived, I commenced cutting the lumber for a drawbridge... In March, 1834, I commenced building it, and I think it was completed by the 1st of June.' Andreas corrects him on the spot: 'Mr. Norton is evidently in error as to the time of the completion of the bridge, since the Democrat states that it was formally accepted by the Trustees in August, the first proposals having been received in February.' The range opens on the LATER of the two, 1 August 1834, because the question a range answers is when the structure certainly stood as a working public crossing, and 'I think it was completed by' is the weaker of the two claims even before Andreas contradicts it. Nothing turns on the choice for this scene: the bridge is standing eleven months before 1835-07-01 either way. THE CLOSE IS THE BEST-ATTESTED DATE ON THIS RECORD: 'the Common Council ordered its removal in July, 1839', and 'a large crowd gathered upon the river before daylight, the next morning, and going to work with a will, in a very short time chopped the bridge to pieces.' A structure destroyed within a day of a dated order is a rarity in this dataset. THE INFERRED TAG IS FOR THE OPENING AND NOT THE CLOSE. The August acceptance rests on an 1834 issue of the Chicago Democrat that this project does not hold, quoted by Andreas fifty years later; the paper itself is the thing that would move this to documented.

position.symbolic_location: Across the main stem of the Chicago River in line with Dearborn Street, its south abutment at the foot of Dearborn on South Water Street.
position.note: PLACED 2026-08-11, AND THE STREET IS BETTER EVIDENCE HERE THAN IT IS ANYWHERE ELSE IN THIS DATASET, because this crossing is named for the street it is on. Andreas has Norton cutting his lumber 'on the land adjoining Michigan Avenue' and the bridge in line with Dearborn; docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 12 puts the south abutment at the foot of Dearborn on South Water Street. METHOD, the same one the North Branch and South Branch records use. The modern Dearborn Street centreline was read from OpenStreetMap at its Randolph Street crossing (node 28290271) and its Kinzie Street crossing (node 4336042974) — two points 528 m apart, straddling the river, on a street that survives on its 1830s alignment; the line through them runs at 359.419 degrees from grid north. Its ends are set where the traced 1834 waterlines cross it: the south bank of the main stem at local E +699.17, N +20.72 and the north bank at local E +698.39, N +97.05, read off data/terrain/epochs/e1834_harbor_cut/shoreline.geojson, which carries the main stem east of the forks box. The value recorded here is the footprint polygon's own origin, which for this crossing is the deck's SOUTH end on its EAST side. Facade bearing 269.419: this archetype's convention is that a deck at rotation 0 runs due east with its upstream side facing north, so a deck running north up the Dearborn line has its upstream (west) elevation facing 269.419 degrees. THE WHOLE STRUCTURE IS OUTSIDE THE MODELLED GROUND. The committed heightfield is a 640 m box centred on the forks and stops at local E +320; this bridge stands at E +699. Nothing in this record is wrong because of that, and everything a visitor would see is: the terrain simply ends 380 m west of the south abutment. Extending the box east is docs/ROADMAP.md S2e, and it is the reason the harbour parcel was held. Working uncertainty about 20 m from the georeference, plus the trace's own; across the river the position is better constrained than along it, because the crossing has to meet both banks.

derivation.reason: This placement predates the derivation module. Its provenance and reasoning are recorded in position.note, but no machine-checkable derivation block has been authored for it yet.

footprint.note: ONE AXIS IS MEASURED AND THE OTHER IS INVENTED, AND THE LEAST CONFIDENT WINS. The length, 76.33 m, is the distance between the two traced 1834 waterlines along the Dearborn alignment, read off shoreline.geojson at the crossing station (south bank local E +699.17, north bank local E +698.39, 76.33 m apart along the street line). That is 250.4 ft of water, and what it is worth is argued on form.overall_length_m, because it is the first independent evidence this project has been able to put against a hundred-and-ninety-year-old disagreement about how long this bridge was. The width, 3.048 m, is not evidence of anything — see form.width_m — so the polygon as a drawn shape is conjectural even though half of it was measured, on the same least-confident-wins rule the mesh uses. WHAT THE MEASUREMENT'S ERROR BAR ACTUALLY IS, and it is smaller than the georeference's headline number. The 20 m stated for anything traced from the 1834 sheets is dominated by a common-mode shift: an affine that puts the whole neighbourhood 20 m north puts both banks 20 m north and the distance between them does not move. What survives into a WIDTH is the sheet's local scale error — the fit records a 3.7 per cent difference between its two axis scales, which is real paper stretch — and the tracing tolerance of 1.78 m. Even a generous ten per cent leaves the water gap above 225 ft. NO SOURCE IS CITED ON THIS BLOCK, DELIBERATELY. The measured axis is argued in this note and cited on form.overall_length_m; a conjectural block carrying a source_id would claim the survey supports a shape it cannot.

construction.note: SAWN AND FRAMED CARPENTRY, NOT THE ROUND LOGS OF THE BRANCH BRIDGES, and the archetype has only two words for it. Norton was a ship-carpenter who 'commenced cutting the lumber for a drawbridge' over the winter of 1833-34 and began building in March: that is a stocked and framed structure, built by a tradesman to a design that won a premium, and it is a different thing from the four heavy logs the settlers describe under the branch bridges. bridge_timber offers 'log' and 'timber_crib' and rejects anything else with the message that a framed bridge is not this archetype; 'timber_crib' is the nearer of the two and it is what the substructure of a low timber causeway across a navigable river in this decade would in fact have been. THE HONEST STATEMENT IS THAT THIS RECORD IS AT THE EDGE OF ITS ARCHETYPE. bridge_timber builds a fixed log stringer crossing; this was a framed timber causeway with a hoisted draw. What it can carry faithfully is the fixed part, and the rest of this form block says which parts of the real bridge are not here at all.

overall_length_m.note: ABOUT THREE HUNDRED FEET, AND THE RIVER AGREES WITH IT. Andreas, History of Chicago vol. 1 (read verbatim in the chicagology transcription; scan p. 415 per docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 4): 'From various sources it is learned that it was about three hundred feet long, and the opening for the passage of craft about sixty feet.' Andreas is hedging — 'from various sources it is learned' means he is reconciling second-hand reports, not reading a specification — which is why the value is recorded in its original unit as about 300 ft rather than as a figure to two decimal places, and 91.44 m is the exact conversion of a number that is itself approximate. THE MEASUREMENT, and it is this record's own contribution rather than another retelling. The distance between the two traced 1834 waterlines along the Dearborn Street alignment is 76.33 m, which is 250.4 ft of open water. That is independent of every text above: it comes from the Wright 1834 segmentation in data/terrain/epochs/e1834_harbor_cut/shoreline.geojson through the same fitted affine that fixes the datum. A bridge about three hundred feet long crossing two hundred and fifty feet of river has about fifty feet of timber over land, twenty-five at either end — which is exactly the long low causeway with approaches that docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 4 describes, and it is a convergence rather than a coincidence: two numbers from unrelated evidence that fit each other without adjustment. THE FIGURE THIS SUPERSEDES, recorded because the project believed it in one of its own dossiers and a reader deserves to know why it went. docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 5 gives the bridge as '200 ft long, 60-ft draw at one end'; its citation is the chicagology page 'The First Bridge Across the Chicago River, 1834', transcribing a 1902 promotional history — 'Chicago Pictorial', Historical Chicago National Bank — whose sentence reads 'The bridge at Dearborn Street was 200 feet long, with a draw of sixty feet at one end.' Two hundred feet is fifty feet SHORTER than the water it would have to cross, so it cannot be a bank-to-bank length, and it is not cited here because this project holds no source record for that 1902 text: naming a source_id that does not resolve would be inventing a citation. THE GEOMETRY DECLARATION says what the model does with all of this. It builds the 76.33 m between the traced waterlines and no approaches, so about a sixth of the length this attribute states is not in the mesh. That is the same missing approach the ground_contact block declares, seen from the other side, and it is admitted in docs/LIBERTIES.md.

draw_span_m.note: SIXTY FEET, AND IT IS THE ONE DIMENSION EVERY TELLING AGREES ON. Andreas: 'the opening for the passage of craft about sixty feet.' The 1902 text that halves the bridge's length keeps the same draw: 'with a draw of sixty feet at one end.' Two accounts that disagree by fifty per cent on the length agree exactly on the opening, which is what a number looks like when it descends from a specification rather than from an estimate by eye. Andreas elsewhere (scan p. 301, per docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 4) records that a premium of twenty-five dollars had been offered for the best plan, 'the draw to be forty feet' — so the built opening was half again what the town asked for. That is a fact about the design competition, not a third figure for the draw. WHAT THE OPENING DOES IN THE MESH: it clears the intermediate supports out of itself and it stations the two gallows frames at its ends. A sixty-foot passage for craft with a pier standing in it is not a passage, so four of the sixteen evenly spaced supports of form.pier_count are dropped, twelve are built, and the deck crosses the opening in one clear run. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO IS OPEN. The draw is built CLOSED, and that is the choice that avoids picking a side in the one thing the sources do not settle — see form.draw_lifting_gear.

gallows_frames.note: TWO TALL TIMBER FRAMES, ONE AT EITHER END OF THE DRAW, AND THEY ARE THE SILHOUETTE THIS BRIDGE IS REMEMBERED BY. Andreas: 'It was of the "gallows pattern," and for five years, the frames, one at either end, stood like instruments of death to frighten the timid stranger at night.' And, of the occasion the machinery jammed: 'for forty-eight hours the gallows frames held the draw suspended in mid-air.' The count and the arrangement are as well attested as anything on this record, and 'either end' is either end of the DRAW rather than of the bridge — the same sentence pairs the frames with the draw hanging between them. THEY ARE BUILT, as of 2026-08-11, and the archetype grew a draw to do it: two heavy posts straddling the deck under a lapped cross-head, at the two ends of the sixty-foot opening. What is documented is how many and where. Everything about their SIZE is conjectural and the whole frame carries that confidence — see form.gallows_height_m — so the feature a visitor sees first is also the one the confidence view dithers hardest, which is the correct way round.

gallows_height_m.note: HOW TALL THE GALLOWS STOOD IS THE MOST VISIBLE UNKNOWN IN THIS DATASET. No source gives the height, the section, the bracing or the tackle of these frames; what survives is that they were tall enough to be frightening at night and strong enough to hold a sixty-foot draw suspended for forty-eight hours. 6.4 m above the deck — about twenty-one feet — is the archetype's own number, chosen so that a frame is unmistakably a gallows against the sky and not a gatepost, and it is not a finding. THE REASON IT IS BUILT AT ALL, rather than declared absent: the confidence view exists exactly for this. A dithered translucent frame says 'this shape is ours' in a way no footnote can, and leaving the frames out would tell a visitor the town's one piece of engineering was a plain causeway, which is a stronger false claim than a tagged guess. The alternative reading was on this record for a few hours on 2026-08-11 and is recorded here because it is a real argument: build nothing, declare it, and let the liberties document carry the frames in prose. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the February 1834 proposals Andreas mentions, the trustees' specification, the twenty-five-dollar premium drawing, or any period view of the river mouth looking west.

draw_lifting_gear.note: A NEGATIVE FINDING, AND A CORRECTION TO THIS PROJECT'S OWN RESEARCH. The draw is repeatedly described in modern retellings, including in docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 5, as DOUBLE-LEAF and as 'opened manually with chains'. NEITHER WORD IS IN ANY UNDERLYING TEXT. Andreas gives 'gallows pattern', the frames 'one at either end', the draw 'hoisted', and the frames holding it 'suspended in mid-air' — which establishes that it lifted rather than swung, and nothing whatever about leaves, chains, ropes or windlasses. On the chicagology page that transcribes him, 'leaves' and 'double-leaf' appear only in descriptions of the 1890s bascule and the 1907 and 1963 bridges, sixty to a hundred and thirty years later; the one windlass on the page belongs to the State Street FERRY rope. Two of the project's own dossiers glossed the same silence in incompatible ways — 03 says double-leaf and chains, 04 models a single hoisted leaf at midstream. THREE READINGS FIT EVERY WORD OF THE EVIDENCE and this record refuses to choose between them: one leaf hinged at one end and hoisted from both frames; two leaves, each hoisted by the frame at its own end; or the whole sixty-foot section lifted bodily between the two frames, which is the most natural reading of 'suspended in mid-air' and the least often repeated. THE MESH IS BUILT TO BE AGNOSTIC. The deck runs continuously across the opening — the draw closed, which is what it was for all but a few minutes at a time — and there is no leaf, no hinge, no chain and no tackle anywhere in it. A raised leaf would have to pick one of the three readings, in the most conspicuous position on the bridge. So the value here is false in the sense that matters: there is no lifting gear in this model, and its form is not evidenced.

width_m.note: NOBODY EVER WROTE DOWN HOW WIDE THIS BRIDGE WAS. Andreas gives its length, its draw, its pattern, its frames, its repairs and its destruction, and not its width; the 1902 text gives length and draw and nothing else; the 1883 old-settlers statement that supplies ten feet for both BRANCH bridges is explicitly about those two and not about this one. THE VALUE IS THE ARCHETYPE'S DEFAULT, KEPT DELIBERATELY RATHER THAN REPLACED WITH A FRESH GUESS — the same choice docs/LIBERTIES.md L29 made about the North Branch bridge's pier spacing, and for the same reason: a new number chosen to look sensible would read as a finding and would not be one. bridge_timber's default is the branch bridges' documented ten feet, which is almost certainly too narrow for the main crossing of the town's principal street, carrying teams, on a structure a shipwright framed to a premium design. It is kept because being visibly the neighbour's number is more honest than being plausibly nobody's. The chip on this row is conjectural and the whole footprint inherits it. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the town trustees' specification, the February 1834 proposals Andreas mentions, or the 1834-35 repair vouchers — the corporation paid $166.67 for repairs in September 1834 and the bridge was repaired again in 1835, and a repair account is the kind of document that states a deck width.

clearance_m.note: SIX FEET, BORROWED FROM THE NEIGHBOURS AND LABELLED AS BORROWED. No source reached states how high this deck stood above the water. The only clearance figure this project holds for any Chicago river crossing of the decade is the 1883 old-settlers statement's 'about six feet above the water' for the two branch bridges, and it is adopted here as an inference from adjacent evidence rather than as evidence about this structure. TWO THINGS SUPPORT THE BORROWING AND ONE COMPLICATES IT. Supporting: the three crossings were built within two years of each other by or for the same corporation, and a bridge that needed a sixty-foot opening for the passage of craft cannot have been high — a high fixed deck is precisely the alternative to a draw, and this town chose the draw. Complicating: the main stem carried masted lake vessels where the branches carried scows and teams, so its bridge had more reason to be built up, and the branch bridges' six feet was set by a use this one did not have, the winter road passing underneath on the ice. The figure is kept because it is the only one there is and because both arguments point low rather than high, and the tag says it is a reading and not a measurement.

deck_kind.note: SAWN PLANK RATHER THAN RIVEN PUNCHEON, AND IT IS THE FIRST RECORD IN THIS DATASET TO CARRY THE VALUE. The branch bridges' floor is documented as 'puncheons or split logs', which is what a crew lays without a sawyer. This bridge was different in the one way that decides the question: Norton 'commenced cutting the lumber' in the winter of 1833-34 and spent three months building from it, to a design that had won a premium, on a structure with a moving leaf. Riven stock of uneven width is not what a ship-carpenter frames a hoisted draw and its approaches from. The mesh differs accordingly — narrower boards, laid regularly, with the ends in line instead of the ragged butts a split floor gives. THE INFERENCE IS FROM THE BUILDER AND THE MATERIAL WORD, not from any statement about the deck, and 'cutting the lumber' could in principle describe felling rather than sawing. It is graded inferred for that reason.

pier_count.note: SIXTEEN SUPPORTS IN THE RIVER, AND NOT ONE OF THEM IS ATTESTED. Nothing anybody wrote describes the middle of this bridge. Something had to hold up 76 m of crossing, so intermediate supports are not the invention; their number, their spacing and their form are. THE VALUE IS THE ARCHETYPE'S FALLBACK MADE VISIBLE. bridge_timber divides a span whose middle nobody described by a 4.5 m default spacing, which over 76.33 m gives seventeen bays and sixteen supports. That fallback exists because of docs/LIBERTIES.md L29, where the same arithmetic put fifteen cribs under the North Branch bridge and the number went unnoticed for a slice because it was hidden in the generator instead of stated on the record. Writing it here as a conjectural count is the repair L29 earned: the same invention, in the open, with a chip on it. Sixteen bents at 4.5 m under a low timber causeway is not an unreasonable trestle for 1834 — which is exactly what makes it dangerous, because a plausible invention is the kind a visitor believes. TWELVE OF THE SIXTEEN ARE ACTUALLY BUILT: four of the evenly spaced stations fall inside the sixty-foot draw and are dropped, because an opening for the passage of craft with a pier in it is not an opening. So the number on this chip is the count the arithmetic produced and not the count in the mesh, and the difference is documented evidence removing an invented support rather than a discrepancy. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the February 1834 proposals, the trustees' specification, or the repair accounts of September 1834 and 1835.

pier_kind.note: NOBODY SAID. The branch bridges' supports are documented as bents of four heavy logs resting on the bottom, because four men who used them wrote it down; nothing equivalent exists for this crossing, and the sentence that would have settled it is the one Andreas did not write. Crib is chosen over the archetype's other two readings — bent and pile — on the ground that it is the archetype's own default and that the harbour works at the mouth of the same river were at that moment being built of timber cribs by federal engineers, in a town whose one shipwright had just framed this bridge. That is a reason to prefer it and not evidence for it, so the tag is conjectural rather than inferred, and the count beside it carries the same chip for the same reason.

ground_contact.note: REGRADED 2026-08-11, and the change of word is the whole point. This phase declared `outside_modelled_ground` because when it was written there was no terrain here at all. S2e has since extended the heightfield east to E +1700, so there IS ground now — and this structure still does not reach it, for the older and more ordinary reason that it stands over water with no modelled approach at either end. A visitor reading the old word would have been told the ground is missing when it is the ramp that is missing. THERE IS NO GROUND UNDER THIS BRIDGE AT ALL, WHICH IS A DIFFERENT AND WORSE FINDING THAN THE ONE BOTH BRANCH BRIDGES MAKE. The committed heightfield is a 640 m box centred on the forks and stops at local E +320; this crossing stands at E +699, three hundred and eighty metres beyond the edge of the world this project has built. Neither the river it spans nor the banks it lands on are modelled here. tools/heightfield.py clamps outside its box rather than extrapolating, so a gate that measured this structure would compare its deck to the elevation of a point four hundred metres away and report a perfect landing on ground that does not exist — which is exactly the failure the `outside_modelled_ground` state was added to make visible. THE SECOND, SMALLER GAP IS STILL THERE UNDERNEATH IT and will surface the moment the terrain reaches this far. Andreas's about-three-hundred feet against a measured 250 ft of water says there WERE approaches — roughly twenty-five feet of timber at either end — and says nothing whatever about what they were made of or how they climbed. When the ground arrives, this declaration becomes `approach_not_modelled` unless somebody has found a description of the landings in the meantime, and the record should not be read as claiming otherwise now. WHAT WOULD SETTLE THIS ONE: docs/ROADMAP.md S2e, which extends the terrain box east to about local E +1560 using the shoreline and harbour vectors already traced and committed in this repository. WHAT WOULD SETTLE THE OTHER: a period depiction, a levelled section, or the trustees' specification. Until then this record is data ahead of ground, which is the right order for a research dataset and the wrong order for a walkthrough. Admitted in docs/LIBERTIES.md.

phases.change_note: The single phase this structure has. Andreas records the bridge as repaired in 1835 and again in 1837, and the September 1834 payment of $166.67 for repairs shows it needed work within weeks of acceptance — so the structure standing on 1835-07-01 was patched and had been struck repeatedly by passing vessels. No source dates or describes any of those repairs closely enough to make a second phase, so the record models one state and says here that it was a worn one.

function.note: A public crossing and the first movable bridge in Chicago: 'The first drawbridge thrown across the river was at Dearborn Street.' It replaced a trustee-established free ferry at the same street — a flat-bottomed boat on a cable, which was moved to Rush Street when the bridge opened — and it was the only fixed link between the North and South Divisions of the town. By the scene date it is also an address: the Chicago American set up its office in June 1835 'on Water Street, near the draw-bridge'.

research_note: CHICAGO'S FIRST MOVABLE BRIDGE, AND THE FIRST RECORD IN THIS DATASET WHOSE OWN MEASUREMENT SETTLES A DISAGREEMENT BETWEEN ITS SOURCES. THE LENGTH, AND WHAT THE RIVER SAYS ABOUT IT. Two figures have been in circulation for over a century: Andreas, 'about three hundred feet long', and a 1902 promotional history — 'Chicago Pictorial', Historical Chicago National Bank — 'The bridge at Dearborn Street was 200 feet long'. This project's own two dossiers took one each, 03 the two hundred and 04 the three hundred, so the disagreement was inside the research before it reached a record. The distance between the traced 1834 waterlines on the Dearborn Street alignment is 76.33 m, which is 250.4 ft of open water, and it is independent of both texts: it comes from the Wright 1834 segmentation through the same fitted affine that fixes the datum. A two-hundred-foot bridge cannot cross two hundred and fifty feet of river. A three-hundred-foot one crosses it with about twenty-five feet of approach at either end, which is what a low timber causeway on a marshy bank looks like. That is a convergence rather than a coincidence, and the value of it is that the two numbers come from evidence that shares nothing — a compiler's reconciliation of pioneer report, and a segmented wash edge on a survey. Recorded on form.overall_length_m; the 1902 text is quoted there and deliberately NOT cited, because this project holds no source record for it and inventing one to make a citation resolve is the worst thing an agent can do here. TWO THINGS EVERY MODERN RETELLING SAYS THAT NO SOURCE DOES, and this record was written with both of them in it before the underlying page was read. The bridge is described everywhere, including in docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 5, as DOUBLE-LEAF and as worked by CHAINS. Neither word is in Andreas's paragraph or in the 1902 text. On the chicagology page that transcribes Andreas, 'leaves' and 'double-leaf' belong only to the 1890s bascule and the 1907 and 1963 bridges, sixty to a hundred and thirty years later — a later bridge's mechanism attached to an 1834 one. What the evidence gives is 'gallows pattern', two frames 'one at either end', a draw 'hoisted', and the frames holding it 'suspended in mid-air': it lifted rather than swung, and that is all. Three arrangements fit every word — one leaf, two leaves, or the whole opening lifted bodily between the frames — and form.draw_lifting_gear records all three and asserts none. WHAT IS BUILT AND WHAT IS NOT. The archetype grew a draw for this record on 2026-08-11: the sixty-foot opening clears four invented supports out of itself, and the two gallows frames stand at its ends. The frames' HEIGHT is conjectural and the whole frame carries that confidence, so the most conspicuous object on the crossing is also the one the confidence view dithers hardest — which is the right way round, and is the reason for building them rather than declaring them absent. Not built: the leaf, the hinge and the tackle, because building any of them picks one of the three readings in the most visible position on the bridge; and the twenty-five feet of approach at either end, which is the same gap the ground_contact block declares. AND THE WHOLE STRUCTURE STANDS OFF THE EDGE OF THE MODELLED WORLD. At local E +699 it is 380 m east of the committed heightfield's boundary. docs/ROADMAP.md S2e has the vectors needed to extend the box to about E +1560 already traced and committed; until that lands, this record is a correct dataset entry and an incomplete thing to look at.
